# Handler in actix_web - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/actix-web/^4/trait.Handler.html

`pub trait Handler<Args>: `[Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + 'static {
    type [Output](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Output);
    type [Future](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Future): [Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html)<Output = Self::[Output](https://docs.rs/trait.Handler.html#associatedtype.Output)>;
    // Required method
    fn [call](https://docs.rs#tymethod.call)(&self, args: Args) -> Self::[Future](https://docs.rs/trait.Handler.html#associatedtype.Future);
}## Expand description

The interface for request handlers.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-a-request-handler)What Is A Request Handler

In short, a handler is just an async function that receives request-based arguments, in any order, and returns something that can be converted to a response.

In particular, a request handler has three requirements:

- It is an async function (or a function/closure that returns an appropriate future);
- The function parameters (up to 12) implement `FromRequest`
- The async function (or future) resolves to a type that can be converted into an
`HttpResponse``Responder`

[§](https://docs.rs#compiler-errors)Compiler Errors

If you get the error `the trait Handler<_> is not implemented`, then your handler does not
fulfill the *first* of the above requirements. (It could also mean that you’re attempting to use
a macro-routed handler in a manual routing context like `web::get().to(handler)`, which is not
supported). Breaking the other requirements manifests as errors on implementing [ FromRequest](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRequest.html)
and

[, respectively.](https://docs.rs/trait.Responder.html)

`Responder`[§](https://docs.rs#how-do-handlers-receive-variable-numbers-of-arguments)How Do Handlers Receive Variable Numbers Of Arguments

Rest assured there is no macro magic here; it’s just traits.

The first thing to note is that [ FromRequest](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRequest.html) is implemented for tuples (up to 12 in length).

Secondly, the `Handler` trait is implemented for functions (up to an [arity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arity) of 12) in a way
that aligns their parameter positions with a corresponding tuple of types (becoming the `Args`
type parameter for this trait).

Thanks to Rust’s type system, Actix Web can infer the function parameter types. During the
extraction step, the parameter types are described as a tuple type, [ from_request](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRequest.html#tymethod.from_request) is run on
that tuple, and the

`Handler::call` implementation for that particular function arity
destructures the tuple into its component types and calls your handler function with them.In pseudo-code the process looks something like this:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
async fn my_handler(body: String, state: web::Data<MyState>) -> impl Responder {
    ...
}
// the function params above described as a tuple, names do not matter, only position
type InferredMyHandlerArgs = (String, web::Data<MyState>);
// create tuple of arguments to be passed to handler
let args = InferredMyHandlerArgs::from_request(&request, &payload).await;
// call handler with argument tuple
let response = Handler::call(&my_handler, args).await;
// which is effectively...
let (body, state) = args;
let response = my_handler(body, state).await;
```
This is the source code for the 2-parameter implementation of `Handler` to help illustrate the
bounds of the handler call after argument extraction:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
impl<Func, Fut, Arg1, Arg2> Handler<(Arg1, Arg2)> for Func
where
    Func: Fn(Arg1, Arg2) -> Fut + Clone + 'static,
    Fut: Future,
{
    type Output = Fut::Output;
    type Future = Fut;
    fn call(&self, (arg1, arg2): (Arg1, Arg2)) -> Self::Future {
        (self)(arg1, arg2)
    }
}
```

# connect in actix_web - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/actix-web/^4/attr.connect.html

`#[connect]`Available on

**crate feature**only.`macros`## Expand description

Creates route handler with `actix_web::guard::Connect`.

[§](https://docs.rs#syntax)Syntax

`#[connect("path"[, attributes])]`[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)Attributes

- `"path"`: Raw literal string with path for which to register handler.
- `name = "resource_name"`: Specifies resource name for the handler. If not set, the function name of handler is used.
- `guard = "function_name"`: Registers function as guard using- `actix_web::guard::fn_guard`.
- `wrap = "Middleware"`: Registers a resource middleware.

[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

Function name can be specified as any expression that is going to be accessible to the
generate code, e.g `my_guard` or `my_module::my_guard`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
#[connect("/")]
async fn example() -> HttpResponse {
    HttpResponse::Ok().finish()
}
```

# main in actix_web - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/actix-web/^4/attr.main.html

`#[main]`**crate feature**only.

`macros`## Expand description

Marks async main function as the Actix Web system entry-point.

Note that Actix Web also works under `#[tokio::main]` since version 4.0. However, this macro is
still necessary for actor support (since actors use a `System`). Read more in the
[ actix_web::rt](https://docs.rs/actix-web/4/actix_web/rt) module docs.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
#[actix_web::main]
async fn main() {
    async { println!("Hello world"); }.await
}
```

- `"path"`: Raw literal string with path for which to register handler.
- `name = "resource_name"`: Specifies resource name for the handler. If not set, the function name of handler is used.
- `guard = "function_name"`: Registers function as guard using- `actix_web::guard::fn_guard`.
- `wrap = "Middleware"`: Registers a resource middleware.

[§](https://docs.rs#notes)Notes

Function name can be specified as any expression that is going to be accessible to the
generate code, e.g `my_guard` or `my_module::my_guard`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
#[options("/")]
async fn example() -> HttpResponse {
    HttpResponse::Ok().finish()
}
```

# routes in actix_web - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/actix-web/^4/attr.routes.html

`#[routes]`**crate feature**only.

`macros`## Expand description

Creates resource handler, allowing multiple HTTP methods and paths.

[§](https://docs.rs#syntax)Syntax

```
#[routes]
#[<method>("path", ...)]
#[<method>("path", ...)]
...
```
[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)Attributes

The `routes` macro itself has no parameters, but allows specifying the attribute macros for
the multiple paths and/or methods, e.g. [ GET](https://docs.rs/attr.get.html) and

[.](https://docs.rs/attr.post.html)

`POST`These helper attributes take the same parameters as the [single method handlers](https://docs.rs/crate#single-method-handler).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
#[routes]
#[get("/test")]
#[get("/test2")]
#[delete("/test")]
async fn example() -> HttpResponse {
    HttpResponse::Ok().finish()
}
```

---

# scope in actix_web - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/actix-web/^4/attr.scope.html

`#[scope]`Available on

**crate feature**only.`macros`## Expand description

Prepends a path prefix to all handlers using routing macros inside the attached module.

[§](https://docs.rs#syntax)Syntax

```
#[scope("/prefix")]
mod api {
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#arguments)Arguments

- `"/prefix"`- Raw literal string to be prefixed onto contained handlers’ paths.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
#[scope("/api")]
mod api {
    #[get("/hello")]
    pub async fn hello() -> impl Responder {
        // this has path /api/hello
        "Hello, world!"
    }
}
```

---

# test in actix_web - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/actix-web/^4/attr.test.html

# Attribute Macro test

[Source](https://docs.rs/actix-web-codegen/4.3.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/actix_web_codegen/lib.rs.html#272) `#[test]`

Available on **crate feature **`macros` only.

## Expand description

Marks async test functions to use the Actix Web system entry-point.

[§](#examples)Examples

```
#[actix_web::test]
async fn test() {
    assert_eq!(async { "Hello world" }.await, "Hello world");
}
```

# axum-core

Core types and traits for axum.

This crate uses `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` to ensure everything is implemented in 100% safe Rust.

axum-core's MSRV is 1.75.
